meta.note: Module numbers for the SBATS base simulation. Every value has a source; a value with no source is null and its module is illustrative. See data/REVIEW_ME.md.
meta.aiAssistance: Compiled with AI assistance (Claude Code) from the cited sources; see AI_USE.md.

oxygenKgPerDay.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 3-31

waterKgPerDay.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 3-31
waterKgPerDay.note: Potable water: 2.00 kg drinking, 0.5 kg food preparation, 0.717 kg extra for exercise. Hygiene water and water recycling are not modelled.

foodKgPerDay.unit: kg dry mass per person per day
foodKgPerDay.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 3-31

oxygenKgPerKgWater.source: Kleinhenz and Paz 2020, Case Studies for Lunar ISRU Systems Utilizing Polar Water, AIAA ASCEND (NASA NTRS 20205007966)
oxygenKgPerKgWater.note: Derived: 13 t of oxygen from 15 t of water in the study's baseline case (13 / 15).

solarConstantWm2.note: Sunlight at Earth's distance, above the atmosphere.

habitat.label: Habitat
habitat.description: Crew quarters, sized on the Mars surface habitat of NASA's Design Reference Architecture 5.0: six crew, about 21.5 t, 12.1 kW.

massKg.source: Drake, Hoffman and Beaty 2010, Human Exploration of Mars, Design Reference Architecture 5.0, IEEE Aerospace Conference (NASA NTRS 20090040343)

crewCapacity.source: Drake, Hoffman and Beaty 2010, Human Exploration of Mars, Design Reference Architecture 5.0, IEEE Aerospace Conference (NASA NTRS 20090040343)
crewCapacity.note: The architecture sends six crew members, housed in one habitat.

powerKw.source: Drake, Hoffman and Beaty 2010, Human Exploration of Mars, Design Reference Architecture 5.0, IEEE Aerospace Conference (NASA NTRS 20090040343)
powerKw.note: 'using 12.1 kWe of electrical power'. Whatever thermal control that figure includes is not broken out.

heatingKwPerDegC.note: No published heat-loss figure per degree was found for a surface habitat. The heating load is not modelled.

comfortTempC.note: Only needed for the heating load, which is not modelled.

solar.label: Solar array
solar.description: One roll-out solar array of the kind added to the International Space Station (iROSA): more than 20 kW in full sunlight at Earth's distance.

massKg.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 3-16
massKg.note: Derived: 16.25 kg per kW (the table's estimate for the ISS roll-out array producing 20 kW, arrays only) x 20 kW.

ratedPowerKw.source: NASA 2021, New Solar Arrays to Power NASA's International Space Station Research, nasa.gov
ratedPowerKw.note: 'Each new solar array will produce more than 20 kilowatts'. Dust and heat on a planet's surface are not modelled.

ratedIrradianceWm2.note: The sunlight the rated power refers to: Earth's distance, above the atmosphere.

battery.label: Battery
battery.description: One lithium-ion battery unit of the kind fitted to the International Space Station: about 15 kWh.

massKg.source: Dalton et al. 2016, International Space Station Lithium-Ion Battery, NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop (NASA NTRS 20170004112)
massKg.note: Derived: specification weight 435 lb x 0.45359 kg per lb.

capacityKwh.source: Dalton et al. 2016, International Space Station Lithium-Ion Battery, NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop (NASA NTRS 20170004112)
capacityKwh.note: 'Li-Ion ~15 kWh'. Depth-of-discharge limits are not modelled.

greenhouse.label: Greenhouse
greenhouse.description: A 50 m2 crop chamber under electric light, with wheat as the reference crop. NASA's Wheeler gives about 50 m2 as the area that feeds one person.

massKg.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 4-88
massKg.note: Derived: 101.5 kg per m2 of growing area x 50 m2.

growingAreaM2.source: Wheeler 2020, Bioregenerative Life Support for Humans in Space (NASA NTRS 20205008786)
growingAreaM2.note: The size chosen for one module: 'about 50 m2' of crops supplies one person's food calories.

foodKgPerM2Day.unit: kg dry edible mass per m2 per day
foodKgPerM2Day.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 4-90
foodKgPerM2Day.note: Wheat: 20.00 g dry weight per m2 per day.

oxygenKgPerM2Day.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 4-91
oxygenKgPerM2Day.note: Wheat: 56.00 g per m2 per day.

waterKgPerM2Day.unit: kg net make-up water per m2 per day
waterKgPerM2Day.note: Wheat takes up 11.79 kg per m2 per day (BVAD Rev 2, Table 4-91), but transpires nearly all of it, and a closed chamber recovers it. No net make-up figure was found, so greenhouse water is left out.

powerKwPerM2.source: NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2 (2022), Table 4-88
powerKwPerM2.note: Lamps, ballasts, root zone and fans. Based on high-pressure sodium lamps; BVAD says it has not been updated for LED lighting, which would lower it.

iceMiner.label: Ice miner
iceMiner.description: A lunar polar water plant sized on NASA's baseline ISRU case: 15 t of water in 225 days from regolith holding 5% ice by mass, with electrolysis to oxygen.

massKg.source: Kleinhenz and Paz 2020, Case Studies for Lunar ISRU Systems Utilizing Polar Water, AIAA ASCEND (NASA NTRS 20205007966)
massKg.note: 'Total Mass 4.9 tons' for the whole plant (ridge system, mine system, two water tankers), without its power system.

waterKgPerDay.source: Kleinhenz and Paz 2020, Case Studies for Lunar ISRU Systems Utilizing Polar Water, AIAA ASCEND (NASA NTRS 20205007966)
waterKgPerDay.note: Derived: 15 t of water collected and processed in 225 days (15,000 / 225). The study assumes 5% ice by mass and 75% extraction.

powerKw.source: Kleinhenz and Paz 2020, Case Studies for Lunar ISRU Systems Utilizing Polar Water, AIAA ASCEND (NASA NTRS 20205007966)
powerKw.note: 'approximately 20 kW' for the water extractor subsystem.

electrolysisKwhPerKgOxygen.source: Kleinhenz and Paz 2020, Case Studies for Lunar ISRU Systems Utilizing Polar Water, AIAA ASCEND (NASA NTRS 20205007966)
electrolysisKwhPerKgOxygen.note: Derived: the electrolysis subsystem draws approximately 20 kW and makes 13 t of oxygen in 225 days (20 kW x 24 h / 57.8 kg per day).

landingPad.label: Landing pad
landingPad.description: A place where a large cargo lander can set down. Cargo per landing is the lower figure NASA gives for its Artemis cargo landers.

massKg.note: No published mass for a prepared lunar or Martian landing pad was found.

cargoKgPerDelivery.source: NASA 2024, Work Underway on Large Cargo Landers for NASA's Artemis Moon Missions, nasa.gov
cargoKgPerDelivery.note: 'approximately 26,000 - 33,000 pounds (12 to 15 metric tons) of payload'. The lower figure is used. A lunar lander; no Mars figure was looked for.

maxSlopeDeg.source: Dwyer Cianciolo 2024, Artemis Human Landing System Update, NASA EDL Summer Seminar (NASA NTRS 20240009596)
maxSlopeDeg.note: 'Surface slope for landing (100m): <10 deg', from a seminar slide of Artemis III requirements, not the requirements document. The site slopes it is compared with are means over a 55 km window at 463 m spacing.

lunarNight.label: Lunar night
lunarNight.description: No sunlight. At low latitudes it lasts 14 Earth days. At a polar site the simulation uses that site's longest dark period instead, where one is published.

durationDays.source: NASA LRO lithograph LG-2013-11-084-GSFC, Temperature Variation on the Moon

solarFactor.source: NASA LRO lithograph LG-2013-11-084-GSFC, Temperature Variation on the Moon
solarFactor.note: Night: the Sun is below the horizon.

marsDustStorm.label: Mars dust storm
marsDustStorm.description: A planet-wide dust storm like that of 2018. Sunlight at the surface falls to a fraction that depends on the site.

durationDays.source: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio 30983 and JPL Opportunity status, 2018 global dust storm
durationDays.note: Derived: the 2018 storm was first detected on 30 May and by 23 July more dust was falling out than being raised (54 days). Dust took until mid-September to clear.

solarFactor.note: No single figure: each Mars site carries its own in sites.<id>.dustStormSolarFactor, from the Mars Climate Database.

irradianceWm2.note: Sunlight at the Moon's distance on an array turned to face the Sun. At the poles the Sun is on the horizon, so arrays stand upright.

litFraction.note: Upper end of the published range for the Shackleton rim (50% to 87% of the time): assumes the arrays stand at the best-lit spot.

longestDarkHours.note: 'longest total darkness about 1.5 days' at the best-lit rim location (1.5 x 24 hours). From the paper's abstract.

iceAvailability.note: No measurement of extractable ice exists for this site. Diviner shows 11.1% of the 55.6 km window never warms above 110 K, where water ice is stable (validation/build/moon_temperature.py). The one direct measurement of lunar polar water, 5.6 +/- 2.9% by mass, is from the LCROSS impact at Cabeus (Colaprete et al. 2010, Science), a different crater.

irradianceWm2.note: Sunlight at the Moon's distance on an array turned to face the Sun. At the poles the Sun is on the horizon, so arrays stand upright.

litFraction.note: Upper end of the published range for Malapert Massif (50% to 82%): assumes the arrays stand at the best-lit spot.

longestDarkHours.note: No published longest dark period for this site was found.

iceAvailability.note: No measurement of extractable ice exists for this site. Diviner shows 1.5% of the 55.6 km window never warms above 110 K, where water ice is stable (validation/build/moon_temperature.py). The one direct measurement of lunar polar water, 5.6 +/- 2.9% by mass, is from the LCROSS impact at Cabeus (Colaprete et al. 2010, Science), a different crater.

irradianceWm2.note: Sunlight at the Moon's distance on an array turned to face the Sun. At the poles the Sun is on the horizon, so arrays stand upright.

litFraction.note: No published share of time in sunlight for this site was found.

longestDarkHours.note: No published longest dark period for this site was found.

iceAvailability.note: No measurement of extractable ice exists for this site. Diviner shows 0.5% of the 55.6 km window never warms above 110 K, where water ice is stable (validation/build/moon_temperature.py). The one direct measurement of lunar polar water, 5.6 +/- 2.9% by mass, is from the LCROSS impact at Cabeus (Colaprete et al. 2010, Science), a different crater.

irradianceWm2.note: Sunlight at the Moon's distance on an array turned to face the Sun. At the poles the Sun is on the horizon, so arrays stand upright.

litFraction.note: The crater floor is in permanent shadow. No published figure for the landing region beside it was found.

longestDarkHours.note: No published longest dark period for the landing region was found.

iceAvailability.note: No measurement of extractable ice exists for this site. Diviner shows 35.4% of the 55.6 km window never warms above 110 K, where water ice is stable (validation/build/moon_temperature.py). The one direct measurement of lunar polar water, 5.6 +/- 2.9% by mass, is from the LCROSS impact at Cabeus (Colaprete et al. 2010, Science), a different crater.

irradianceWm2.note: Sunlight at the Moon's distance on an array turned to face the Sun.

litFraction.note: Derived: away from the poles, open ground is in daylight for half of each lunar day of 29.53 Earth days (synodic period, NSSDC). Hills that shade the site are not modelled. Arrays on the surface; nothing inside the pit is lit.

longestDarkHours.note: Derived: half of the 29.53-day lunar day (29.53 x 24 / 2 = 354 hours). The same night the LRO lithograph rounds to 14 Earth days.

iceAvailability.source: LRO Diviner Global Cumulative Products, PDS LRO-L-DLRE-5-GCP-V1.0 (validation/build/moon_global_temperature.py); Horvath, Hayne and Paige 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49:e2022GL099710, doi:10.1029/2022GL099710
iceAvailability.note: Inferred, not measured: Diviner measures the open surface here at 392 K at midday, far above the 110 K below which water ice stays put, and a model of a similar pit gives about 290 K in its shadowed interior (Horvath et al. 2022). No one has looked for ice inside this pit.

irradianceWm2.source: Mars Climate Database v6.2 (LMD/OU/IAA/ESA/CNES), incident solar flux on a horizontal surface (validation/build/mars_sunlight.py)
irradianceWm2.note: Climate model, not a measurement. Mean over the Mars year, seasons weighted by their length. Mean flux on flat ground while the Sun is up.

litFraction.source: Mars Climate Database v6.2 (LMD/OU/IAA/ESA/CNES), incident solar flux on a horizontal surface (validation/build/mars_sunlight.py)
litFraction.note: Climate model, not a measurement. Mean over the Mars year, seasons weighted by their length. Share of local hours with any sunlight.

longestDarkHours.source: Mars Climate Database v6.2 (LMD/OU/IAA/ESA/CNES), incident solar flux on a horizontal surface (validation/build/mars_sunlight.py)
longestDarkHours.note: Longest night of the Mars year, from hourly model output: good to about an hour.

iceAvailability.source: Piqueux et al. 2019, Geophysical Research Letters 46:14290, doi:10.1029/2019GL083947
iceAvailability.note: Inferred, not measured at the site: shallow ground ice is reported at latitudes as low as 35 N and 45 S, and Jezero is at 18 N.
